articles.author: Tina Schuchman CVP, Foundry and Vladimir Fedorov, CTO, GitHub
articles.body: If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. But building one that works seamlessly across multiple models and surfaces is incredibly hard. You need to solve for performance, quality, and cost. And then you have to maintain it, which is even harder. Luckily, the GitHub engineering team built a best-in-class, truly multi-model harness, which we’ve adopted company-wide. The Microsoft Copilot harness powers Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, the GitHub Copilot app, the CLI, VS Code, and more. And today, we’re making that harness available through Microsoft Foundry. That gives developers and enterprise customers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. You get the right model for the job without switching the harness or the rest of your tech stack. That frees up your time, energy, and resources to focus on your bottom line. What’s a harness, and why is it hard? If the model supplies the intelligence, the harness is everything around the model. It’s the orchestration layer that gives an agent the right instructions, context, execution environment, and controls to accomplish meaningful work. And a harness worth its salt has support for open standards like MCP and agent skills, as well as agent plugins. This is a fast-moving space. A frontier model today might fall behind tomorrow. And building your own harness or model router to keep up can be painful and slow. Now, you can build on the same harness Microsoft and GitHub ship in our own products, and you don’t have to maintain it. We invest in science and engineering work to continually improve and evolve the harness and ensure high-quality, efficient, and low-cost performance across a range of models and workloads. The benefits compound for us and our customers who use the harness to build and run their own agents. Improve the harness, and every surface it touches benefits. Born in GitHub, battle-tested at enterprise scale The Copilot harness was built by the same GitHub engineers behind new technologies like our multi-model orchestration. And those technologies are only possible because we built our own harness. Designed to be fast, token-efficient, and predictable, it was our original, high-quality harness. articles.title: The CISO’s evolving role: Protecting and defending in the agentic era
articles.summary: As AI and agents reshape the enterprise, CISOs face two critical priorities: enabling innovation with the right identity and data guardrails, and modernizing defense to keep pace with AI-powered threats. Aarti Borkar shares how security leaders can approach both. The post The CISO’s evolving role:...
articles.author: Aarti Borkar
articles.body: October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it’s a good time to think about how much the world has changed for chief information security officers (CISOs) in the last 12 months. A year ago, we thought we were already in the thick of AI and starting to understand it. Since then, agents have spread across the enterprise faster than most organizations anticipated. According to our Work Trend Index Annual Report, the number of active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15-fold year over year and 18-fold in large enterprises. Employees are building and deploying AI systems that can access company data, interact with applications, and take actions on their behalf. These systems are built with good intentions, but even well-intentioned agents can introduce risk when access and behavior are not appropriately governed. At the same time, more people inside our companies are building with AI. Many of them haven’t written code in years, if ever, and they aren’t necessarily thinking about security the way a security team would. That isn’t a criticism. It’s how quickly the technology has expanded who can build and what they can accomplish. For CISOs, this creates two fundamental shifts. We have to protect an enterprise that increasingly operates through AI and agents. And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale. When I talk with CISOs, these are the two challenges I keep coming back to. We need to enable innovation without introducing unmanaged risk, and we need to modernize defense without losing the security fundamentals that still matter. Get the 2026 Work Trend Index report For builders: Build securely in the agentic era Cybersecurity awareness has always been about people. This year, it has to include the people building agents. If you’re a developer, a builder, or someone who has just realized that AI can help you design and build things, this part is for you. Give your agents their own identities. Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. When something goes wrong, you need to know which agent did it and be able to shut it off. Protect the data your agents touch. If an agent can reach information, assume it will use it. Make sure the right data protections are in place before you connect it. And remember that the agent will not think like you. It doesn’t share your judgment or your sense of what is appropriate. articles.author: Google Cloud
articles.body: Published: 2026-10-23Updated: 2026-10-27Description Description Severity Notes On Saturday, October 17, 2026, Google received a report from a security researcher regarding the compromise of private keys associated with eight eMudhra subordinate Certification Authority (CA) certificates, including those cross-signed by AAA Certificate Services. Consequently, these CA certificates are no longer trusted and are being revoked. Although Google Cloud infrastructure remains uncompromised, the following Google Cloud and Firebase products, base images, and client SDKs are impacted: Google Cloud CLI Cloud Shell Container-Optimized OS Compute Engine Google Kubernetes Engine Vertex AI Colab Enterprise App Engine Cloud Run Cloud Run functions Cloud Functions for Firebase Firebase AppHosting Cloud SQL AlloyDB Cloud Firestore Firebase App Distribution Cloud Monitoring Confidential Space Google Distributed Cloud What should I do? Google Cloud is actively managing this issue across our infrastructure and platform services, and Google Cloud infrastructure has not been breached. Security telemetry shows no evidence of exploitation against Google Cloud workloads, and proactive mitigations are in place across Google-managed environments to block and distrust the affected certificate authority certificates. For environments and dependencies that you manage directly, take the following actions: Operating Systems & Self-Managed Environments: If you manage operating systems or custom container images on Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), or Cloud Run, update the trust store via your operating system vendor to revoke trust in the compromised eMudhra (emSign) and AAA Certificate Services certificates: Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL): Follow RHSB-2026-012. Debian: Update to the latest ca-certificates package (Bug 1151446). Ubuntu: Follow USN-8944-1. Windows: Install the latest Windows updates. Container-Optimized OS (COS): Upgrade or restart nodes to pick up current COS milestone releases, or apply the cos_ca_cert_mitigation tool. Google Cloud CLI: Update to the latest gcloud CLI release to ensure bundled dependencies include updated certificate stores. Service-Specific Guidance: For managed Google Cloud and Firebase services, such as Google Kubernetes Engine, Serverless runtimes, Managed Databases, Cloud Firestore, Firebase App Distribution, and Confidential Space, Google Cloud is rolling out updates across managed fleets, and service-specific details, release notes,...

Google Cloud backend services are not directly impacted, and no action is required to secure the underlying Google Cloud infrastructure. However, customers hosting Next.js applications on Google Cloud must take immediate action to secure their own workloads. We recommend that you manually upgrade your Next.js deployments to one of the following versions (or later) in your package.json: 16.3.3 15.5.24 Customers utilizing libheif should monitor for upstream OS patches and rebuild their container base images accordingly. Redeploy your updated workloads to ensure running containers utilize the patched versions. What vulnerabilities are being addressed? The vulnerabilities, GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 and GHSA-g89c-p67h-r497, allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code within the context of the application by supplying a crafted image file during Next.js image optimization. articles.author: IustinIrimia
articles.body: Attacks rarely stay in one channel. A flood of spam email, a Teams chat from an unfamiliar organization, and a call from "the helpdesk" can all be part of the same attempt. Security teams need a unified way to see where attacks are happening across email and collaboration, investigate them quickly, and show whether their defenses and users are improving. That's the job of our Detections and Insights reports. They're ready-to-use templates that turn Defender's email and collaboration data into views your team can use every day, as a Microsoft Sentinel workbook or a Power BI report. Today we're releasing version 4, which builds on Part 3 of this series, with new hunting queries and a new report for attack simulation training. Shaped by customer feedback, it helps you: See the attacks that matter with new Teams and impersonation views. Investigate faster with 125 new or improved hunting queries. Measure and improve resilience with a new attack simulation training report. See the attacks that matter In September, Microsoft Threat Intelligence described a campaign that starts on Teams: an attacker from another organization poses as IT support in a chat or call and talks the user into a remote session. Spotting activity like this early means looking at Teams alongside email. The new Teams & Collaboration view puts those Teams signals in one place: threats in chats and channels, callers and senders with support-style names such as "IT Helpdesk", new external senders, risky links, and the calls and messages users reported. A new Email – Impersonation & BEC tab in the workbook does the same for email, highlighting impersonation attempts that reached an inbox and the people they targeted. Each major workbook tab now opens with key numbers and recommended actions, so the team can go from "what happened?" to "what should we check next?" in one place. In Microsoft Sentinel, the workbook can also combine several workspaces in one view, which helps managed security service providers (MSSPs) and organizations with many tenants. The Teams & Collaboration view and the Email – Impersonation & BEC tab, shown with test data from a lab tenant. Investigate faster When something needs a closer look, the next questions come quickly. Has this sender contacted us before? Did anyone report a call from them? Are several addresses using the same "IT Helpdesk" display name? To help answer them, we added 71 new hunting queries for email and collaboration and improved 54 existing ones....

[What and why]Users will soon be able to register a passkey as their first multifactor authentication method. articles.body: Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​ Introduction Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities. Read more on the PHP official website. Microsoft has been part of the coordinated industry response to these vulnerabilities, working alongside the PHP Foundation, Wiz, security researchers, and other industry partners to help protect customers. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations against known exploitation patterns to provide an additional layer of protection while customers apply the PHP security updates. These protections are intended to complement patching and are not a replacement for it. articles.author: yuvalpery
articles.body: Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 contain a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, according to the recently published CVE-2026-111497. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially run arbitrary code. Any application that decompresses untrusted Brotli data may be affected. This includes Node.js and Python applications that bundle the vulnerable decoder, and services that accept request bodies with the Content-Encoding: br header. We strongly recommend upgrading Brotli to a patched version: 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1 (Brotli releases). If you use Node.js, upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 (Node.js security release). If you can't patch your applications right away, Azure WAF on Application Gateway, Application Gateway for Containers and Azure Front Door can help mitigate the inbound attack vector, which is Brotli-compressed request bodies sent to your application. Note: Azure WAF inspects only inbound requests to your application. It can't protect applications that fetch and decompress Brotli-encoded responses from external servers. Those applications must be patched. Built-in protection enabled by default If you use Azure WAF with DRS 2.2, on Application Gateway or Azure Front Door Premium, you're protected by default against the crafted requests we analyzed. Rule 920450 (Paranoia Level 1, enabled by default) checks requests against a list of restricted headers, and DRS 2.2 adds Content-Encoding to that list. The rule has a critical anomaly score, so a single match blocks the request when the WAF policy is in Prevention mode. Earlier rule set versions don't restrict this header. If you're still on DRS 2.1, CRS 3.2 or earlier, we recommend upgrading to DRS 2.2 to get the latest protection. To learn how, see Upgrade CRS or DRS ruleset version. articles.body: Amy Coleman, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer, shared the below communication with Microsoft employees today. Today, we’re introducing a new Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to eligible employees within participating organizations. This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs. The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter. This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program. What employees should know This offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below. This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs. Eligible employees will receive an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details within the next few hours. Looking ahead The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute. My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving. Thank you for everything you continue to do for our customers, Microsoft and for one another. articles.summary: Hi all. Jerry Devore dropping in for a minute to share some insights about the BlockNtlmv1SSO setting that went into effect with the October 2026 update. Why the change was necessary When MS-CHAPv2 is used for solutions like VPN, Wi-Fi, NPS, and RADIUS, the authentication flow leverages the MD4...
articles.author: JerryDevore
articles.body: Hi all. Jerry Devore dropping in for a minute to share some insights about the BlockNtlmv1SSO setting that went into effect with the October 2026 update. Why the change was necessary When MS-CHAPv2 is used for solutions like VPN, Wi-Fi, NPS, and RADIUS, the authentication flow leverages the MD4 hash of the account’s password to respond to a challenge. If that sounds familiar, then you have at least a basic understanding of NTLM. The problem is that this relic from 1998 (NT 4.0 SP4) produces a response to the challenge that is cryptographically equivalent to NTLMv1. So, while a device using MS-CHAPv2 can have NTLMv1 disabled, it is still exposing the same type of challenge response that makes NTLMv1 trivial to crack. The Change B ack in August 2025, an update added support for the registry setting BlockNtlmv1SSO (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0). The update did not create the registry setting, but it caused devices to start auditing for the use of "NTLMv1-derived credentials". With the October 2026 update, the default for Windows devices is to block the use of NTLMv1-derived credentials. This means that organizations that are still dependent on CHAPv2 are going to be impacted. Bracing for Impact For organizations that have already blocked NTLMv1 in their domains, there is no required action because MS-CHAPv2 using domain credentials is already impossible. For everyone else, you might want to do your due diligence before letting the October update rip if you are not certain whether you have any dependencies on MS-CHAPv2. The documentation for this change mentions events 4024 (Warning) and 4025 (Error) which are logged to the NTLM log of the client (Microsoft-Windows-NTLM/Operational). Those events are extremely helpful, but very few organizations are forwarding the client NTLM logs to their SIEM. Possibly a better approach The October 2026 update giveth and the October update taketh away. What do I mean by that? Besides taking away NTLMv1-derived credentials, the update backported the enhanced NTLM auditing events to Server 2019 and Server 2022. As a result, you can leverage your domain controllers’ logs to determine if you have any MS-CHAPv2 dependencies prior to updating your endpoints. Here is an example of a 4033 event logged on a domain controller when the VPN server forwarded the challenge response for "credential validation". We can tell this was CHAPv2 because a true NTLMv1 authentication would have populated the other...

articles.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzes the LiteLLM 1.107.0 compromise, including Python startup hooks, credential theft, remote code loading, detections, and mitigations. The post Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks appeared first on...
articles.author: Microsoft Security Research, Mahesh Mandava, Srinivasan Govindarajan, Sagar Patil and Suriyaraj Natarajan
articles.body: In this article Attack overview Technical detailsMitigation and protection guidanceIndicators of compromiseReferencesLearn More On October 21, 2026, a compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release was published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) and distributed through official container images. The malicious package added files that Python could execute during normal interpreter initialization. An application did not need to import LiteLLM for the payload to run: starting Python in an affected environment could be enough. Microsoft analyzed two execution paths in the affected wheels: a credential collector launched through a path extension, and a Unix-oriented loader persisted through site-specific configuration. The collector targeted authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. A separate database module attempted to read selected credential and model-configuration records from the LiteLLM proxy. Endpoint observations on Windows and macOS matched the recovered collector’s discovery, encryption, and outbound-connection behavior. In one Windows example, a routine Python invocation to install an unrelated dependency activated the collector. This distinction matters for response: investigators should not start Python or pip inside a suspect environment to determine whether the malicious package is present. This blog explains the startup mechanisms, the credentials the payload could reach, and the evidence defenders can use to investigate exposure. It also provides Microsoft Defender detection information, advanced hunting queries, and recovery guidance. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery. Organizations must address the affected Python environment, any surviving processes, and credentials accessible to the compromised identity. Attack overview LiteLLM is commonly deployed as a gateway between applications and model providers. In that position it may have access to model-provider API keys, database connection strings, workload identities, routing configuration, and tenant policy data. The same package is also used on developer workstations, build agents, test systems, and containers, which widened the set of environments that could be exposed by the compromised release. articles.author: Microsoft Security Research and Microsoft Threat Intelligence
articles.body: In this article What’s happeningWhat is ARTEX?Mitigation and protection guidanceReferencesLearn more As early as September 2026, Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. Microsoft assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply chain compromise of a multi-tenant application. This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially. Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises. Storm-0940’s use of ARTEX accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to Microsoft 365 customer environments through applications that had already been granted access. This allowed the threat actor to operate without requiring an interactive user sign-in. In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access. The activity conducted by the threat actor through the usage of ARTEX framework did not result from a compromise of or a vulnerability in Microsoft corporate systems, products, or services. Although Microsoft identified Storm-0940-initiated authentication and follow-on activity in multiple customer environments, the presence of an affected application or successful threat actor authentication does not necessarily indicate that customer data was accessed or exfiltrated. articles.body: In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge will compound as models become even more powerful. While most have been worried about threat actors using powerful models to attack, the focus has been less on agents within our own walls. Since we were the ones who deployed agents internally for our companies, we implicitly trusted our agents. Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted. This is not because models are inherently malicious. Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment. Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised. Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise. They are agentic insiders. Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly. To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7. An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime. In July, we announced Project Perception, an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise. articles.author: Michael Scovetta
articles.body: The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments. While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time. As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks. Today, Microsoft and NVIDIA are publishing Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, the first in a planned series of joint resources intended to help enterprises address those questions. The paper introduces a shared risk taxonomy and an approach to managing model risks grounded in established standards and frameworks, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework. The paper reflects a core idea: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards. Read the whitepaper: Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise Understanding risk in the deployment context Open- and closed-weight models can share many of the same underlying risks, but how those risks materialize depends on the deployment. A model used to help an employee draft a document presents different considerations than the same model used in a customer-facing workflow, just as a standalone inference endpoint differs from a system connected to external data or tools. The architecture matters too. A risk may originate in the model, while the most effective control may sit in the inference environment, application, or surrounding operational processes. The joint guidance looks beyond the model label to factors including provenance, intended use, users, deployment conditions, and surrounding controls. articles.author: Megha_Priya
articles.body: As more developers begin to use Linux desktops, they become more attractive to attackers: high-privilege, high-value, and easy for admins to overlook. A developer using Linux for day-to-day development may interact with source code repositories, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, cloud infrastructure, container environments and internal development platforms. If their workstation is compromised, an attacker doesn’t just gain access to a laptop, but a foothold in the pipelines that build and ship the organization’s software. As Linux adoption expands beyond the data center, organizations need a consistent approach to protecting Linux wherever it is used. articles.body: By: Christian Friedel-Jain - Sr. Security Consultant | James Noyce - Sr. Security Solution Engineer Introduction Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) are among the most sensitive endpoints in any organization. A PAW, in most of our Microsoft consulting projects, exists to do one job safely: administer cloud services from a hardened device that is only ever allowed to reach a small, tightly controlled set of internet destinations. But an endpoint’s security posture is ultimately defined by its behavior under failure conditions. When we moved the internet access restriction for our PAW devices from a locally enforced restriction (more about that later) to a solution based on Microsoft Global Secure Access (GSA), we immediately identified a gap under failure conditions – but first a quick grounding on the moving parts. Global Secure Access (What is Global Secure Access?) is Microsoft’s umbrella term for Microsoft Entra Internet Access and Microsoft Entra Private Access — the components of Microsoft’s Security Service Edge solution. For a PAW device we are leveraging Microsoft Entra Internet Access as an identity centric secure web gateway solution to control exactly which internet destinations the workstation can reach, by applying a fine-grained set of rules and policies enforced through Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra. This configuration provides us better filtering capabilities, like web content filtering (Global Secure Access web content filtering) with TLS inspection (TLSi) (Global Secure Access transport layer security inspection) and additional features like Threat Intelligence (Global Secure Access threat intelligence), but it comes also with a downside. Currently by default, if the GSA client encounters an issue or cannot connect to its required GSA edge services, the GSA client will fall back to a fail-open state, rather than to a fail-close state. Difference between those two modes: Fail-Open: When a security or control mechanism fails, access is still allowed. Fail-Close: When the security or control mechanism fails, access is blocked. This blog post covers above problem and showcases a solution we built, as part of our projects, to achieve a “Fail-Close” state rather than having the current “Fail-Open” behavior. Certificates, trust anchors, PKI services, applications, devices, and hardware security modules may all be affected by new algorithms and larger certificate chains. By the end of this article, security leaders, public key infrastructure (PKI) administrators, and architects will understand the key certificate dependencies, migration risks, and practical first steps for post-quantum authentication readiness. Why post-quantum authentication presents a different challenge Much of the current PQC readiness discussion focuses on confidentiality and the ‘harvest now, decrypt later’ risk, in which adversaries collect encrypted data today with the expectation that future quantum computers could decrypt it. articles.summary: Potentially Unwanted Applications, or PUA, they aren't necessarily malware, but they are applications you probably don't want running across your environment either. Microsoft defines potentially unwanted applications as software that can adversely affect endpoint performance or use. Examples...
articles.author: Vytas_Boyev
articles.body: Potentially Unwanted Applications, or PUA, they aren't necessarily malware, but they are applications you probably don't want running across your environment either. Microsoft defines potentially unwanted applications as software that can adversely affect endpoint performance or use. Examples include advertising software, software bundlers, and applications that use behaviors intended to evade security products. Microsoft Defender can also consider an application's reputation when determining whether software qualifies as potentially unwanted. That sounds straightforward. On Windows, it generally is. On Linux, finding the resulting audit events requires knowing exactly where to look. And that is where things get interesting. PUA, PUP… Same Neighborhood, Slightly Different Address Before going further, it is worth clearing up some terminology. Across the security industry, you will commonly encounter both PUP, or Potentially Unwanted Program, and PUA, or Potentially Unwanted Application. The terms are frequently used for software that isn't necessarily malicious but has characteristics that make its presence undesirable, such as intrusive advertising, bundling additional software, or other behavior the user might not have knowingly requested. Microsoft uses Potentially Unwanted Application (PUA) as its product and detection terminology. Microsoft specifically distinguishes PUA from malware. A PUA might cause poor system performance, display unexpected advertisements, install other software, or have a poor reputation because of undesirable behavior, but those characteristics don't automatically make the application malware. articles.author: JamesAde
articles.body: Email remains one of the most common entry points for security threats. Yet email products often describe the same activity with different table names, fields, and values. This makes it harder to build detections and investigations that work consistently across data sources. The Microsoft Sentinel Advanced Security Information Model, or ASIM, EmailEvent schema is now available. It provides a common structure for email delivery and inspection events, helping customers and partners create security content that works across supported email data sources. A consistent view of email security activity EmailEvent standardizes the information analysts need to understand what happened to an email and why. It covers: Email delivery and inspection events Sender, source, and recipient information Message subject, size, direction, and delivery location URLs and file attachments SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication results Delivery actions such as delivered, blocked, quarantined, or deleted Threat, risk, confidence, tactic, technique, and remediation details Instead of learning a different data model for every product, analysts can query the normalized EmailEvent fields. Parser developers map each source's native data to the same schema. How it works Consider an email that contains a suspicious attachment. The email security product records the sender, recipients, attachment, authentication results, inspection verdict, and final action. A connector collects that event. A parser or Data Collection Rule maps the source fields to EmailEvent. Microsoft Sentinel can then query the normalized record using the same field names used for other supported email sources. This common structure separates security content from the details of a specific product. When another source adds an EmailEvent parser, existing source-independent queries and detections can work with that source without being rewritten around its native field names. Why it matters Simpler analytics: Write queries against one consistent set of email fields. Broader coverage: Apply source-independent security content across normalized email sources. Faster investigations: Compare delivery, authentication, attachment, URL, and threat details without translating different data models. Easier integration: Give connector and parser developers a defined contract for bringing new email telemetry into ASIM. EmailEvent does not replace the rich native data produced by email security products. It provides a consistent...

articles.author: Freddy Dezeure and Sesha Mani
articles.body: Most of what has been written about AI and vulnerability management focuses on speed: how much faster frontier AI models can scan code, find weaknesses, design patches, and build exploits than any human team. That part is true, and it matters to how we remediate vulnerabilities. The more challenging question is what happens after the scan? Frontier AI models are about to hand every security team a far larger set of findings than they have ever had to work through. The real test for chief information security officers (CISOs) and IT security leaders is not how fast they can patch. It is whether they can keep the balance between patching quickly and patching correctly, at a scale no human review process was built for. This shift creates both new challenges and new opportunities. The same AI capabilities accelerating cyberattackers are also enabling defenders to identify exposures earlier, automate remediation, and build more resilient security programs. Not every vulnerability will be patched in time, so the controls that limit what an attacker can do by defense in depth matter more than ever. CISOs can dramatically improve the security posture of their Microsoft infrastructure by deploying Microsoft Baseline Security Mode (BSM), building on how Microsoft protects Microsoft. Learn more about Microsoft Baseline Security Mode How do frontier AI models change vulnerability management for CISOs? Microsoft uses frontier AI models to find vulnerabilities in its code base and mitigate them at controlled pace. Potential vulnerabilities are reviewed on validity, severity, and potential impact. As we have explained in previous blogs, many steps in our vulnerability handling and disclosure processes now are AI-powered, allowing them to scale. Most vulnerabilities in cloud software are being mitigated by Microsoft without customer intervention. For on-premises Microsoft software, customers should continue to expect a substantial increase in the number of vulnerabilities released on Patch Tuesdays relative to historic volumes before the advent of frontier AI models earlier this year—September 2026 saw a record number, close to 1,000.1 Due to the non-deterministic nature of AI models, different runs by the same model or with different models may yield different results. articles.summary: The real problem isn't WHOIS. It's what WHOIS costs you at scale. Ask any SOC analyst whether WHOIS data is useful and they'll say yes without hesitation. articles.author: absharan
articles.body: The real problem isn't WHOIS. It's what WHOIS costs you at scale. Ask any SOC analyst whether WHOIS data is useful and they'll say yes without hesitation. Registrant emails, creation dates, registrars, and nameservers are among the most durable pivots in domain-based threat intelligence — the threads that tie a single phishing domain back to an entire adversary campaign. Now ask them how often they actually pull WHOIS for every suspicious domain in an alert. The honest answer is: not always. And that gap is the real problem. Here's why. When a campaign surfaces two hundred lookalike domains, manual WHOIS becomes a losing game: It's slow. One-domain-at-a-time portal lookups don't finish before the incident clock runs out. It's inconsistent. Different analysts capture different fields, so the data can't be compared or correlated. It's un-auditable. Screenshots and copy-paste don't hold up in an investigation review months later. It loses the pattern. By the time you've checked twenty domains by hand, the shared registrant email that connected them has scrolled off the screen. The outcome of all this friction is the part that should worry a security leader: analysts quietly stop enriching, or enrich only a sample. The pivot that would have collapsed twenty alerts into one campaign never happens. The newly registered domain that should have been escalated gets triaged as routine. The intelligence exists — the process just can't reach it fast enough. The outcome we're actually after Reframe the goal. This isn't a project to "run WHOIS." It's a project to produce a specific set of outcomes: Every suspicious domain gets enriched — not a hand-picked sample. Enrichment is consistent and structured, so patterns across domains become visible instead of buried. The output is audit-ready — defensible in an investigation and reusable in a report. The whole thing is fast enough to happen inside the incident, not the day after. Get-MDTIWhois.ps1 exists to deliver exactly those outcomes. It reads a list of domains, calls Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence (MDTI) through Microsoft Graph, and returns both a normalized CSV for immediate triage and the raw JSON for deep investigation — in one pass, read-only, with nothing changed in your environment. What changes for the analyst The clearest way to see the value is the before-and-after. Before: An alert fires on a suspected phishing campaign with two hundred candidate domains. articles.body: Satya Nadella, Chairman and CEO, and Ryan Roslansky, Executive Vice President of LinkedIn and Microsoft 365, shared the below communications with Microsoft and LinkedIn employees this morning. SATYA NADELLA MESSAGE After nearly 18 years at LinkedIn and Microsoft, Ryan Roslansky has decided to leave Microsoft and embark on his next chapter. As Ryan and I have been discussing our roadmap and work ahead, we felt this was the right moment for this change. Ryan will stay through the end of the calendar year as an advisor to me and will support on the transition. Ryan leaves the organization in a strong position. With Copilot, we are executing rapidly against our vision to build a new OS for work that spans every model, every form factor, and every task, with Office fully embedded in Copilot and vice versa! Over the past year, Ryan’s team has done critical work bringing together the product, engineering, and design foundations that have made this next phase possible. Last week’s launch was an important milestone in that journey, and the strong response from customers, partners, and the broader ecosystem reinforced both how far we’ve come and how much opportunity remains ahead. At LinkedIn, we remain focused on our core vision of creating economic opportunity for every member of the global workforce, helping our 1.3 billion members access the knowledge, insights, and opportunities they need to navigate rapidly changing professional and labor markets. Effective today we will make the following changes: Sumit Chauhan and Lan Ye will report to Charles Lamanna. Jon Friedman will report to Jacob Andreou. Dan Shapero will continue as CEO of LinkedIn and Mohak Shroff will continue in his role, both reporting to me. Over his nearly two decades at Microsoft, Ryan has helped shape how people around the world find opportunity, build their careers, and get their work done. articles.author: Matthew Thomas
articles.body: According to this year’s Microsoft Digital Defense Report, government agencies and services were the sector most impacted by cyber threats in 2026, accounting for 27% of observed activity, up from 17% in 2025. Governments are also the most frequently targeted sectors for nation-state activity. They are attractive targets because they hold sensitive information, operate essential services, and sit at the center of networks of agencies, contractors, technology providers, and critical infrastructure operators. Dwell time, the period between when an attacker gains access and when defenders detect and stop them, also increased this year across multiple sectors. While organizations responded faster once an intrusion was identified, detecting threats early remains a challenge. Attackers increasingly gain access through techniques that mimic legitimate activity, making malicious behavior harder to spot. For example, phishing accounted for 23% of observed intrusions in 2026, up from 7% in 2025, highlighting the continued importance of compromised identities as an entry point for broader attacks. Taken together, the implication for governments is clear. Security in the AI era is no longer simply about preventing individual intrusions. It is about ensuring institutions can operate effectively in an environment where risks are interconnected, threats move faster, and attackers remain hidden longer. Public-private partnerships are also more important than ever for securing critical government infrastructure and developing the policies and regulations needed for emerging technologies. In this year’s report, which examines cyber threat trends observed between July 2025 and June 2026, Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s Corporate Vice President & Deputy Chief Information Security Officer, and I explore how these dynamics are reshaping cyber risk. In a companion blog, Terrell takes a closer look at what these findings mean for CISOs and security professionals. A vulnerability’s discovery in the wild to active weaponization can be well below 24 hours. While the number of publicly disclosed software vulnerabilities (commonly tracked as CVEs) is projected to reach a record 72,000 in 2026. articles.body: In April, I published a set of referential architecture diagrams for Microsoft Purview — Microsoft Purview Referential Architecture Diagrams. They have been useful in workshops and training sessions for a simple reason: one picture is worth a thousand words - attempting to explain the complex in a single image. Today I'm publishing an update focused on classification and labeling — and on the wave of public previews that make auto-labeling something you can scale across the entire estate with ease. Detailed view mode ➡️ Download the interactive architecture on GitHub here. It's a self-contained HTML file - and it's a lot more than this picture! Why now: auto-labeling scales to the whole estate The most consequential change is surprisingly small. An auto-labeling policy can now be kept on while you edit it, without re-triggering simulation. Anyone who has run auto-labeling at scale knows why that matters. Until now, tuning a policy meant turning enforcement off, re-simulating, waiting, and turning it back on — delays every time you refined a rule. That friction made it challenging for organizations from broadening scope as fast as they wanted to. Removing it changes the operating model: you can simulate once with your conditions and expand scope (sites) when you're ready, without hitting the simulation limit. It arrives alongside a set of previews that lift every ceiling that used to cap the motion: Capacity is up 5x. Auto-labeling for SharePoint and OneDrive moves from 100,000 to up to 500,000 files per tenant per day (Roadmap ID 567890). Simulation goes from 4M to 20M items, so you can model against a real estate rather than a sample. Policy scope gets much bigger. Select up to 1,000 individual SharePoint sites per policy, adaptive scopes support up to 50,000 sites, and you can filter sites by the SiteTemplate property when configuring a policy (Roadmap ID 570445, MC1469958). Reporting finally tells you what happened. Audit and reporting now summarize the sensitive information types detected when labels are applied, and a new 30-day chart shows files processed per day so you can watch policy throughput. articles.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence examines CVE-2026-73570 exploitation in Zimbra, including observed attack paths, detection opportunities, and mitigation guidance. articles.author: Microsoft Security Research, Mahesh Mandava and Rajesh Kumar Natarajan
articles.body: In this article Attack chain overviewMitigation and protection guidanceReferencesLearn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified and tracked exploitation of CVE-2026-73570, an unauthenticated OS command injection vulnerability in the Zimbra Collaboration Suite SNMP notification path. Exploitation can be triggered by a specially crafted email against internet-facing Zimbra servers when the optional zimbra-snmp package is installed and SNMP notifications are enabled, without requiring authentication or user interaction. Following successful exploitation, observed activity included deployment of JSP web shells and reverse shells, privilege escalation, persistent remote-access tooling, and memory-backed execution. Threat actors also accessed email and collected authentication and mailbox data, with archive creation and subsequent transfer activity observed. The activity included both automated payload delivery and hands-on-keyboard operations on compromised mail servers. Microsoft observed affected organizations in more than one region and industry. Based on the environments investigated, exploitation was not limited to a single sector or geographic area. The diagram combines behaviors observed across multiple confirmed compromises; no single host necessarily exhibited every stage. From remediation to public disclosure CVE-2026-73570 is an unauthenticated OS command-injection vulnerability in the Zimbra Collaboration Suite SNMP notification path. An attacker can send a specially crafted SMTP request that introduces untrusted input into SNMP notification processing. If the input is not sufficiently sanitized, embedded shell commands can execute with the privileges of the zimbra service account. Exploitation requires the optional zimbra-snmp package to be installed and SNMP notifications to be enabled. Zimbra version 10.1.20, released July 20, 2026, contains the relevant remediation. CVE-2026-73570 was publicly disclosed on August 13, 2026. Microsoft telemetry identified activity targeting the same injection path during the interval between those events. articles.body: The Microsoft Purview architecture diagrams provide a referential view of how data classification, sensitivity labeling, Data Loss Prevention (DLP) and Insider Risk operate across Microsoft 365 workloads. These diagrams are intended to help organisations understand where policy evaluation occurs, how signals flow between services, and how enforcement is applied consistently. Rather than prescribing a single deployment model, the diagrams illustrate common architectural patterns used to protect sensitive data across endpoints, email, and collaboration services. 2026-09-09 - New Classification and auto-labeling interactive referential architecture now available here: Scaling classification and labeling: an interactive reference architecture update | Microsoft Community Hub. Classification: How Content Sensitivity Is Determined This diagram shows how content is classified across Microsoft 365 workloads and connected locations. Key points highlighted in the diagram: Classification can occur in the client, in transport, or in the service, depending on workload and policy. Multiple classifier types are supported, including Sensitive Information Types (SITs) - deterministic patterns and keywords, and several advanced classifier models such as Exact Data Match, document fingerprinting and trainable classifiers. Classification informs about what's in the content and results are reused by downstream controls such as DLP, auto-labeling, data lifecycle management, eDiscovery and more. Classification is performed real time or near real time as content is created, modified, or transmitted. Classification acts as the core signal for Purview data protection. All enforcement decisions shown in later diagrams rely on these classification outcomes. Sensitivity Labelling: A Unified Control Plane The labeling diagram illustrates how sensitivity labels are applied and enforced consistently across Microsoft 365. Key points highlighted in the diagram: Labels are organizational signals. they are end user facing and provides a consistent approach in training users on data security hygiene. They are your unified control plane across your data estate. Labels can be applied manually, with layered defaults, and/or automatically, depending on workload and configuration. Labels travel with content across SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, Outlook, Office apps and more. articles.title: Phishing Abuses RMM Tools for Persistent Access
articles.summary: Microsoft observed phishing campaigns that abused MSP360 RMM to deploy ScreenConnect, creating redundant remote-access channels for follow-on activity The post Phishing Abuses RMM Tools for Persistent Access appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
articles.author: Microsoft Security Research, Parasharan Raghavan, Deva Kanna Kannan, Sai Chakri and Microsoft Defender Experts
articles.body: In this article Attack chain overviewMitigation and protection guidanceLearn More In July 2026, Microsoft Defender Experts observed phishing campaigns targeting organizations across multiple industries that distributed a masqueraded MSP360 Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) installer through meeting invitations, PDF-themed lures, software update prompts, and other social-engineering content. Once executed, the legitimate MSP360 installer, distributed under a deceptive file name established remote management access on affected devices and enabled threat actors to gain an initial foothold using trusted administrative software. Microsoft observed the MSP360 deployment being used to download and install a ConnectWise ScreenConnect client, creating a secondary remote-access channel that provided redundant access to compromised systems. Microsoft did not observe exploitation of ScreenConnect software itself; rather, threat actors abused legitimately obtained remote administration software to establish and maintain access. After access was established, threat actors used these remote administration channels to deploy additional tools and conduct post-compromise activity, including information collection and credential-access operations. This activity highlights how threat actors continue to abuse legitimate remote administration software to blend into normal IT operations while maintaining persistent access and reducing detection opportunities. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint detects suspicious and uncommon remote-management activity, while the hunting queries and mitigations in this post can help organizations identify and restrict unapproved RMM use. Attack chain overview The observed multi-stage intrusion chain began when phishing lures delivered a legitimate, digitally signed MSP360 RMM v2.5.0.67 installer under deceptive filenames. Following successful User Account Control (UAC) elevation, the installer established MSP360 services for persistent access and leveraged the RMM agent to invoke PowerShell, download, and silently install ConnectWise ScreenConnect. This effectively introduced a second remote administration channel on the compromised device, which the threat actor subsequently used to transfer and execute additional tooling supporting credential access, local data collection, and other post-compromise activity. articles.body: In this article Star Blizzard TTPs observed in 2026Defending against Star Blizzard and RedFlick-related activityMicrosoft Defender detectionsHunting queriesIndicators of compromise Since January 2026, Microsoft has observed Russian state threat actor Star Blizzard evolve their detection evasion capabilities through large-scale phishing campaigns, the use of accounts on compromised websites, and a novel malware delivery technique that Microsoft tracks as “RedFlick”. These changes represent a notable shift in the actor’s operational tradecraft and support ongoing cyberespionage activity targeting Ukrainian individuals and institutions as well as international non-government organizations (NGOs), Western think tanks, governments, and other organizations associated with international policy—particularly those with a nexus in supporting Ukraine. As part of this evolution, Star Blizzard adopted RedFlick, a malware delivery technique that helps evade detection by initiating a set of scheduled tasks to deploy the actor’s custom backdoor, CosmicPulse. This technique is a notable departure from the actor’s previous use of ClickFix-based infection chains which required victims to complete multiple actions before CosmicPulse could be installed. By contrast, the RedFlick infection flow only requires a single user interaction, reducing friction in the compromise process. Combined with the actor’s shift toward large-scale phishing operations during the same period, these changes likely improve Star Blizzard’s ability to reach more targets, evade detection, and increase the likelihood of successful compromise. This blog provides updated technical analysis of Star Blizzard’s tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed throughout 2026, building on our 2025 and 2023 blogs. It details the actor’s evolving phishing, persistence, and malware delivery techniques, and provides recommendations, indicators of compromise (IOCs), detections, and hunting guidance to help organizations identify and defend against RedFlick-related activity. As with any observed nation-state actor activity, Microsoft directly notifies customers that have been targeted or compromised, providing them with recommendations and mitigations to secure their accounts.
